content: 1. Chibwesha CJ and colleagues conducted a randomized trial to evaluate the effectiveness of point-of-care early infant HIV diagnosis. This study highlights the potential of rapid diagnostic tools in improving early detection and treatment outcomes for HIV-infected infants. 2. Spooner E and collaborators implemented a study to identify best practices for point-of-care HIV testing in early infant diagnosis. Their findings, published in BMC Public Health, emphasize the importance of integrating rapid diagnostic methods into healthcare systems to enhance accessibility and timeliness of care. 3. Technau KG and colleagues assessed the Xpert HIV-1 point-of-care test for neonatal HIV diagnosis within a maternity hospital's birth testing program. Their field evaluation, published in The Lancet HIV, demonstrated the feasibility and clinical utility of this diagnostic approach. 4. Le Roux SM and Vojnov L reviewed the cost-effectiveness of point-of-care nucleic acid testing for early infant HIV diagnosis compared to centralized laboratory-based testing. Their systematic review of mathematical modeling studies underscores the economic and clinical benefits of decentralized testing strategies. 5. Salvatore PP and colleagues modeled the cost-effectiveness of point-of-care platforms for infant HIV diagnosis in sub-Saharan Africa. Their study, published in AIDS, provides evidence supporting the scalability of these platforms in resource-limited settings. 6. De Broucker G and collaborators evaluated the cost-effectiveness of scaling up rapid point-of-care testing for early infant HIV diagnosis in southern Zambia. Their findings, published in PLoS One, highlight the economic and public health advantages of expanding access to rapid diagnostic tools. 7. Frank SC and colleagues conducted a modeling study to assess the clinical impact and cost-effectiveness of incorporating point-of-care assays into early infant HIV diagnosis programs in Zimbabwe. Their results, published in The Lancet HIV, support the integration of these assays to improve health outcomes. 8. McCann NC and collaborators compared the strengthening of existing laboratory-based systems versus investing in point-of-care assays for early infant HIV diagnosis. Their cost-effectiveness analysis, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, provides insights into optimizing resource allocation for HIV diagnostic services. 9. A multi-country affordability analysis conducted by the Clinton Health Access Initiative examined the financial feasibility of point-of-care infant diagnosis across four sub-Saharan African countries. The findings emphasize the importance of cost considerations in scaling up diagnostic interventions. 10. Katirayi L and colleagues explored caregivers' and community members' perspectives on the use of point-of-care early infant HIV diagnosis. Their qualitative study, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, revealed a strong preference for same-day results to reduce anxiety and improve care engagement. 11. Bianchi F and collaborators assessed the acceptability of routine point-of-care early infant HIV diagnosis among clinical and laboratory personnel in eight African countries. Their qualitative findings highlight the importance of training and support for healthcare workers to ensure successful implementation. 12. Ochodo EA and colleagues conducted a systematic review of point-of-care tests detecting HIV nucleic acids for diagnosing HIV infection in infants and children aged 18 months or less. Their review, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, provides evidence for the diagnostic accuracy and utility of these tests. 13. The WHO HIV/AIDS diagnostics technology landscape report outlines the current state of diagnostic tools and their potential for improving early detection and treatment of HIV. This document serves as a critical resource for policymakers and healthcare providers. 14. Ethical and equity considerations regarding the implementation of novel HIV/AIDS diagnostics are discussed in the updated WHO recommendations. These guidelines emphasize the need for equitable access to innovative diagnostic approaches to achieve global health targets. 15. Essajee S and colleagues highlighted the role of innovative diagnostic approaches in reducing mortality among HIV-infected infants and achieving the 90-90-90 targets. Their study, published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society, underscores the importance of early and accurate diagnosis in improving survival rates. 16. Kuhn L and collaborators investigated the relationship between early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) and negative HIV antibody results in children with suppressed viral loads. Their findings, published in AIDS, provide insights into the immunological outcomes of early ART initiation. 17. Payne H and colleagues analyzed the reactivity of routine HIV antibody tests in children who initiated ART in early infancy as part of the CHER trial. Their retrospective analysis, published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases, highlights the challenges of interpreting serological results in this population. 18. Deeks JM and Perez Gonzalez M conducted a systematic review of rapid antibody tests for diagnosing HIV exposure and infection in infants and children. Their unpublished findings contribute to the evidence base for selecting appropriate diagnostic tools. 19. Hsiao N and colleagues evaluated the Alere q point-of-care test for early infant HIV diagnosis in South Africa. Their study, published in PLoS One, demonstrated the test's accuracy and operational feasibility in a real-world setting. 20. Sanders GD and collaborators performed an economic analysis of strategies to improve HIV testing and receipt of results. Their study, published in the Journal of General Internal Medicine, provides a framework for evaluating the cost-effectiveness of diagnostic interventions. 21. Schackman BR and colleagues assessed the cost-effectiveness of rapid syphilis screening in prenatal HIV testing programs in Haiti. Their findings, published in PLoS Medicine, highlight the potential for integrated diagnostic approaches to improve maternal and child health outcomes. 22. Uzochukwu BS and collaborators conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of rapid diagnostic tests, microscopy, and syndromic approaches for malaria diagnosis in Nigeria. Their study, published in Malaria Journal, has implications for scaling up diagnostic interventions in resource-limited settings. 23. Batwala V and colleagues compared the cost-effectiveness of malaria microscopy and rapid diagnostic tests versus presumptive diagnosis in Uganda. Their findings, published in Malaria Journal, support the use of diagnostic tools to improve malaria control efforts. 24. Mazanderani AH and collaborators reported on declining baseline viremia and increasing discordant HIV-1 confirmatory results within South Africa's early infant diagnosis program. Their study, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, highlights the evolving challenges in HIV diagnostics. 25. Feucht U and colleagues discussed the implications of false-positive HIV DNA PCR testing in infants within a changing epidemic. Their study, published in the South African Medical Journal, emphasizes the need for confirmatory testing to ensure accurate diagnosis. 26. The guidelines for the use of antiretroviral agents in pediatric HIV infection provide comprehensive recommendations for diagnosing and managing HIV in infants and children. These guidelines are a critical resource for clinicians and healthcare providers. 27. Mazanderani AH and collaborators proposed recommendations for managing indeterminate HIV PCR results within South Africa's early infant diagnosis program. Their study, published in the South African Journal of HIV Medicine, provides practical guidance for addressing diagnostic uncertainties. 28. Luo R and colleagues conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the use of an indeterminate range in HIV early infant diagnosis. Their findings, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, inform strategies for improving diagnostic accuracy. 29. Luzuriaga K and Mofenson LM discussed the challenges in eliminating pediatric HIV-1 infection. Their review, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, highlights the barriers to achieving global elimination goals. 30. Salvatore P and colleagues modeled the clinical consequences of using an indeterminate range for early infant HIV diagnosis. Their study, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, provides evidence for optimizing diagnostic algorithms. 31. Migone C and Ghardshenas A contributed to the updated WHO recommendations on antiretroviral regimens and early infant HIV diagnosis. Their work emphasizes the importance of evidence-based guidelines in improving health outcomes. 32. Violari A and colleagues investigated the time to viral rebound after stopping ART in children treated from infancy in the CHER trial. Their findings, presented at the CROI conference, provide insights into the long-term outcomes of early ART initiation. 33. The WHO consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery, and monitoring provide a comprehensive framework for addressing the HIV epidemic. These guidelines emphasize the importance of combination prevention strategies tailored to local epidemiology and context. 34. Behavioral interventions, such as targeted information and education programs, can reduce the frequency of potential HIV transmission events. These programs leverage various communication approaches, including social media and mobile technology, to reach key populations. 35. Enabling interventions that address structural barriers to accessing services can increase uptake and adherence to prevention, testing, and treatment services. These interventions address critical social, legal, and political factors contributing to HIV transmission. 36. The WHO guidelines on voluntary medical male circumcision recommend its promotion as an additional HIV prevention option for adolescent boys and adult men in settings with generalized epidemics. This intervention has been shown to reduce the risk of heterosexual HIV acquisition by approximately 60%. 37. Embedding voluntary medical male circumcision service delivery within the overall health system is key to achieving sustainability and aligning with global efforts to strengthen health systems and achieve universal health coverage. 38. Behavioral interventions, such as school-based comprehensive sexuality education and peer counseling, play a critical role in HIV prevention. These programs disseminate targeted messages and promote safer sexual practices. 39. Structural interventions, such as legal and policy reforms, gender equality promotion, and economic empowerment, are essential for creating an enabling environment for HIV prevention and care. 40. The WHO is in the process of updating its guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, and service delivery to reflect broader health considerations and emerging evidence.
